title: Memoize II
statement:
Write `memoize(fn)`, which returns a **memoized** version of `fn`: a function that returns what `fn` would return, but runs `fn` at most once for any list of arguments. When it is called with arguments that match an earlier call, it hands back the result stored for that call and does not run `fn`. Two argument lists match when they have the same length and their arguments are pairwise `===`. So two separate objects never match, even with equal contents, while passing the very same object again does. `fn` may take any number of arguments of any type and may return any value.

Each case gives:

- `fn`, the name of the function: `"sum"` adds up its arguments (all numbers; `0` when there are none), `"merge"` returns a new object with the properties of all its arguments (later arguments override earlier ones), and `"list"` returns a new array of its arguments.
- `objects`, a list of JSON objects and arrays. Each one becomes a single real object, created once for the whole case.
- `inputs`, the argument lists of the calls, in order. An argument `{ "ref": i }` stands for the object `objects[i]`, the same object every time it appears; any other argument is that JSON value itself (a number, string, boolean or `null`).

The judge calls the memoized function with each argument list in turn and records `{ val, calls }`: the value it returned and how many times `fn` has run so far. The answer is the list of these records.
constraints: inputs holds at most 10^5 arguments in total
Each argument is a number, a string, a boolean, null or { "ref": i } with 0 <= i < objects.length
Numbers are integers from -10^9 to 10^9 (never NaN)
For "sum" every argument is a number; for "merge" every argument refers to an object that is not an array
signature: List<Object> memoize(String fn, List<Object> objects, List<List<Object>> inputs)
notes:
## Intuition

The cache has to be keyed by a whole argument list, compared argument by argument with `===`. Turning the list into a string does not work: `JSON.stringify` gives two different `{}` objects the same key, and a plain join mixes up `1` and `"1"`. A `Map`, however, compares its keys by identity (like `===`, and `NaN` never appears here), so any single value, object or not, can be a key. To key on a **list** of values, nest the Maps into a trie: the first level branches on the first argument, the next level on the second, and so on. The node reached at the end of an argument list holds that list's result. (The brute force keeps every earlier call and compares lists element by element: also correct, but O(number of calls) per lookup.)

## Approach

1. `root` is the trie node of the empty argument list. Every node has `children` (a `Map` from the next argument to the next node), `done` (has `fn` run for this exact list?) and `value` (its result).
2. On a call, start `node` at `root`.
3. For each `arg` in order, create the child for `arg` if it is missing, then move `node` to it.
4. If `node.done` is false, run `fn(...args)` once, store the result in `node.value` and set `node.done`.
5. Return `node.value`.

## Example 1, step by step

`fn` is `sum`.

- `(2, 2)`: from `root`, a child for `2` is created, then another child for `2` under it. That node is not done, so `sum` runs: `val` 4, `calls` 1.
- `(2, 2)`: the same path exists and its node is done, so 4 comes back while `calls` stays 1.
- `(1, 2)`: a new child for `1` under `root`, then one for `2`; `sum` runs: `val` 3, `calls` 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k) per call with k arguments, since each `Map` lookup or insert is O(1) on average; plus one run of `fn` per new argument list.
- Space: O(total number of arguments over the distinct argument lists), one trie node per new argument.

## Pitfalls

- Keys from `JSON.stringify(args)` treat equal-looking objects as the same: Example 2 would wrongly report 1, 1, 1 calls.
- Joining the arguments into a string mixes up `1` and `"1"`, or `(1, 23)` and `(12, 3)` without a separator.
- Testing `if (node.value)` for a hit reruns `fn` whenever the result is falsy, such as `sum()` = 0; keep the separate `done` flag.
- `(1)` and `(1, 2)` share a path, so a node can have children **and** a result of its own; do not store results only at leaves.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `fn` | the function being memoized |
| `root` | trie node for the empty argument list, shared by every call |
| `args` | the arguments of the current call |
| `node` | the trie node reached so far along `args` |
| `arg` | the argument used to choose the next child |
| `children` | `Map` from an argument to the next trie node |
| `done`, `value` | whether `fn` has run for this node's argument list, and what it returned |

narration.1: memoize runs once per function and sets up the cache shared by every call.
narration.2: root is the trie node for an empty argument list; nothing is cached yet.
narration.3: Each call of the memoized function arrives here with its arguments.
narration.4: Start walking the trie from its root.
narration.5: Go one level deeper for each argument, in order.
narration.6: A Map compares keys by identity, so a new object or value has no child yet.
narration.7: Create the node for this argument so the path can continue.
narration.9: Step into the node for this argument.
narration.11: The node is not done: fn has never run for exactly these arguments.
narration.12: Run fn once and keep its result in the node.
narration.13: Mark the node so later calls with the same arguments skip fn, even if the result is falsy.
narration.15: Return the stored result, whether it was just computed or cached.
